title: Stairs: The Glory of the Ordinary

source.pdf_page_offset_note: PDF page 1 is the summary sheet; printed body page numbering begins on PDF page 2.

context_sources.use: Official task, measurement constraints, and deliverable requirements.

limitations: PDF pages 1, 2, 5, 8, and 18 are image-layer pages with no usable extracted text and were read from full-resolution renders.
Many equation glyphs are absent from extracted text; central formulas were checked visually.
The paper contains a repeated third-party watermark and does not include code, raw images, fitted data, or Monte Carlo samples.
All 25 pages were visually reviewed through contact sheets, with key image-only and equation pages checked at full resolution.

primary_predictions: Infer stair usage frequency from wear patterns.
Infer whether people traveled single file or side by side.
secondary_guidance: Assess consistency between observed wear and known age or use history.
Assess consistency with a proposed stone quarry or wood source.
Distinguish short high-volume use from long low-volume use.
measurement_constraints: Performable by a small team with minimal tools.
task_reconstruction.paper_case: The paper selects interior stairs of the Leaning Tower of Pisa as a single case and treats image-derived wear depth as the central observation.

section_map.summary: Compresses the image-processing, wear, traffic, age, renovation, source, and sensitivity results.
Maps preparation, two model families, sensitivity analysis, conclusion, references, and appendix.
Frames archaeological value and begins a nine-item task restatement.
Maps task groups to wear analysis, characteristic analysis, material comparison, and flow models.
Shows a detailed model flowchart and begins four simplifying assumptions.
Defines variables and applies grayscale conversion and Gaussian denoising.
Extracts an image-derived surface and assumes a bivariate normal wear-depth shape.
Describes PSO least-squares fitting and reports fitted bivariate-normal parameters.
Displays fitted 3D/2D wear surfaces and introduces Archard-style wear inference.
Inverts wear depth to estimate 1,175 daily users and compares with an annual visitor count.
Defines an edge-wear preference index and predicts predominantly descending travel.
Introduces a pedestrian continuity model under continuous-medium and no-slip assumptions.
Discretizes the continuity equation, infers single-file use, and assumes exponentially decaying traffic.
Integrates traffic decay and derives theoretical wear depth.
Compares theoretical and image-derived wear, sets an MSE threshold, and begins inverse age estimation.
Uses differential error propagation and outlines Monte Carlo age estimation.
Reports a 95 percent age interval and lists portable repair-detection measurements.
Defines stone and wood feature sets using scans, material properties, and dating concepts.
Uses Pearson correlation across material feature vectors and asserts a Carrara source.
Displays a radar chart and formulates uniform versus impulse-like traffic wear.
Compares two-day wear, asserts long uniform use, and begins sensitivity analysis.

Shows a map connecting Pisa and the Carrara quarry.

contributions.summary: Creates a low-cost image-to-wear pipeline and represents the wear surface with a fitted bivariate normal form.
Inverts an Archard-style wear relationship to estimate average daily pedestrian traffic from integrated wear depth.
Defines a directional wear index from asymmetric step-edge wear to infer ascending versus descending preference.
Uses a source-augmented pedestrian continuity equation and finite differences to classify single-file versus parallel passage.
Combines inverse age estimation, first-order error propagation, and a Monte Carlo interval.
Translates renovation inference into a practical list of non-destructive scans and surface tests.

nodes.label: Processed stair images and inferred wear surface
Bivariate normal wear surface with PSO fit

assumptions.summary: The archaeologist can obtain any measurement considered important.
assumptions.consequence: Measurement availability is treated as unconstrained beyond later prose, although the official task imposes cost, team-size, and non-destructive constraints.
assumptions.verification: Not tested; carbon-14 dating later conflicts with a strict non-destructive interpretation.

assumptions.summary: All shoe-step friction coefficients are equal.
assumptions.consequence: Footwear material, sole pattern, contamination, and individual variation are collapsed into one wear coefficient.
assumptions.verification: The paper acknowledges violations but performs no sensitivity or subgroup test.

assumptions.summary: All people apply equal pressure on each step.
assumptions.consequence: Body mass, gait, posture, carried loads, and ascent/descent force differences are omitted.
assumptions.verification: No pressure distribution data or violation test is supplied.

assumptions.summary: Relative friction distance is equal for everyone.
assumptions.consequence: Stride, cadence, contact time, and center-of-mass differences are ignored.
assumptions.verification: No sensitivity analysis is tied to this assumption.

assumptions.summary: A single-person, single-center bivariate normal distribution represents long-term wear depth.
assumptions.consequence: Multimodal lanes, two feet, edge effects, repairs, and changing traffic patterns are collapsed into one smooth mode.
assumptions.verification: Only visual similarity to one processed image is reported.

assumptions.summary: Wear is modeled as a power-law function of pedestrian count with constant material/environment parameters; step deformation, temperature, elasticity, and inter-step differences are ignored.
assumptions.consequence: Age, traffic, load, material, environment, and renovation become weakly identifiable from one wear snapshot.
assumptions.verification: One aggregate visitor-count comparison is used.

assumptions.summary: Pedestrians are treated as a continuous medium with no-slip behavior at walls.
assumptions.consequence: Discrete lane formation and wall avoidance are replaced by density and velocity fields.
assumptions.verification: No pedestrian trajectory or density dataset is used.

assumptions.summary: Daily use decays exponentially after construction.
assumptions.consequence: The inferred age and cumulative wear depend strongly on an unobserved social-history curve.
assumptions.verification: The curve is motivated by life experience rather than historical data.

assumptions.summary: A short crowd peak is approximated by an impulse and is assumed to cause more wear than the same total traffic distributed over time.
assumptions.consequence: Peak-versus-uniform classification depends on an asserted nonlinear crowd-wear relation.
assumptions.verification: No calibrated contact-load or congestion-wear law is supplied.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Uses an unspecified image of a Leaning Tower stair, converts it to grayscale, applies Gaussian denoising, performs edge detection, and selects the bottom step because it has the best processing effect.
data_and_preprocessing.risk: No camera calibration, scale calibration, perspective correction, depth sensor, image provenance, or selection criterion is documented.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Fits bivariate-normal parameters rho, means, and standard deviations with PSO minimizing unnormalized least-squares error.
data_and_preprocessing.risk: The reported error 35.562 is called small without sample size, units, scale, baseline, or residual diagnostics.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Uses completion year 1370, exponent b=0.3, step area 0.8 m^2, and k=0.06; the text describes k both as a wear coefficient and as a friction coefficient.
data_and_preprocessing.risk: Conflating friction and wear coefficients makes dimensions and physical interpretation unclear.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Claims wear depths from 100 steps at the same location but provides no table, acquisition protocol, or raw measurements.
data_and_preprocessing.risk: The stated sample cannot be independently verified.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Uses density, wear rate, Mohs hardness, porosity, and penetration as stone-source features and proposes tree-ring/crack/fiber/dating features for wood.
data_and_preprocessing.risk: Features have heterogeneous units, ranges, and uncertainty; collection methods and normalization are not specified.

models.summary: A normalized bivariate Gaussian is used as the stair wear-depth surface and fitted by PSO least squares.
models.purpose: Turn a processed image into a compact spatial wear representation.
models.algorithm: Gaussian denoising, edge extraction, depth reconstruction, PSO least-squares fitting.
failure_modes: normalization inconsistent with physical depth units

models.summary: An Archard-inspired power law d=kN^b is inverted and integrated over step area to estimate daily traffic.
models.purpose: Infer usage frequency from accumulated wear.
failure_modes: non-identifiability of age, load, material, environment, and traffic

models.summary: A preference index compares wear at different edge locations and uses its sign to infer direction.
models.purpose: Infer ascent/descent preference from asymmetric edge wear.

models.summary: A source-augmented continuity equation evolves pedestrian density with flux divergence under no-slip boundaries and a finite-difference scheme.
models.purpose: Classify single-file versus parallel use from density.
models.algorithm: Forward Euler in time and central differences in space.
failure_modes: called Navier-Stokes without a momentum equation
heatmap scale inconsistent with reported density

models.summary: Exponential decay in traffic is integrated into cumulative wear and inverted for service life.
models.purpose: Check wear consistency and estimate stair age.
failure_modes: inconsistent conclusions from the two age views

models.summary: First-order differential error propagation and random parameter sampling are used to report an age interval.
models.purpose: Quantify reliability of the inverse age estimate.
failure_modes: confidence interval formula mixed with Monte Carlo narrative

models.summary: Pearson correlation across a short heterogeneous feature vector is used as a material-source similarity score.
models.purpose: Assess whether stairs match Carrara stone or candidate wood.
failure_modes: invalid p-value interpretation for feature matching

models.summary: Uniform traffic and an impulse-like crowd peak are assigned different wear expressions and compared using consecutive-day scans.
models.purpose: Distinguish short high-volume use from long low-volume use.
failure_modes: daily wear change likely below image resolution

verification.summary: The fitted 3D and top-down surfaces are judged visually close to the processed image.
verification.limitation: No residual map, held-out pixels, normalized error, or uncertainty is shown.

verification.summary: Estimated daily traffic 1,175 is compared with 500,000 annual climbers, or about 1,370 per day.
verification.limitation: Modern tourist traffic is not necessarily representative of historical average traffic, and the source is not fully documented.

verification.summary: A separate-up/separate-down staircase description is used to support the inferred descending direction.
verification.limitation: The architecture can make direction inference circular because the sampled staircase's function may already be known.

verification.summary: Theoretical 654-year wear of 4.871 cm is compared with image-derived 4.5 cm, and MSE=0.1542 is compared with a chosen 0.2 threshold.
verification.limitation: The threshold, 100-step sample, calibration, and MSE units are not justified or shown.

verification.summary: A Monte Carlo plot is said to keep T within a 95 percent interval and reports 282.1984-342.8016 years.
verification.limitation: Inputs, distributions, iteration count, output sample, and coverage test are absent; a draw lying inside an interval derived from the same draws does not establish reliability.

verification.summary: A known renovation history is cited after inverse age is much less than tower age.
verification.limitation: The same paper earlier calls theoretical and actual wear consistent, creating an unresolved interpretation conflict.

verification.summary: Strict timed-entry management is used to support the long-duration low-volume classification.
verification.limitation: Current visitor policy does not validate historical traffic distribution or the consecutive-day wear equation.

verification.summary: Selected wear-shape and traffic-source parameters are varied and outcome plots are shown.
verification.limitation: The paper equates large output changes with high sensitivity but does not assess whether that is desirable robustness or instability.

results_trace.summary: Image-derived wear and a power-law inversion yield 1,175 users per day, used as stair usage frequency.
results_trace.uncertainty: Strongly dependent on uncalibrated k, b, age, depth scale, and historical traffic assumptions.

results_trace.summary: A negative directional index is interpreted as a preference for descending.
results_trace.uncertainty: No measurement-error or alternative-geometry analysis is reported.

results_trace.summary: Reported density rho=0.6535 below 1.5 is mapped to single-file travel.
results_trace.uncertainty: The PDE closure, scale, thresholds, and heatmap values are not reconciled.

results_trace.summary: Theoretical and image-derived wear are declared consistent using MSE=0.1542<0.2.
results_trace.uncertainty: Raw observations and threshold basis are missing.

results_trace.summary: Inverse age is 312.5 years with a reported 282.1984-342.8016 interval; the gap from 654 years is then used to infer renovation.
results_trace.uncertainty: The inference conflicts with the preceding consistency claim and does not isolate renovation from traffic/material error.

results_trace.summary: Feature correlation and external historical knowledge are used to assert Carrara quarry origin.
results_trace.uncertainty: The statistical comparison is not validly specified and partly confirms already known provenance.

results_trace.summary: A reported comparison 0.205<0.241 plus current visitor policy supports long-duration low-volume use.
results_trace.uncertainty: No actual consecutive-day wear measurements or uncertainty are supplied.

writing_logic.summary: Nine prompt questions are grouped into preparation, wear analysis, characteristic analysis, and sensitivity tasks.
The workflow visually distinguishes preparation, two main model families, and sensitivity analysis with method labels at each handoff.
A literary quotation and historical paragraph interrupt the transition from fitted wear data to Archard's law without adding model evidence.
A low inverse age is interpreted as renovation even though the previous section declares observed and theoretical wear consistent.
The conclusion lists model families but does not close every official question with the numeric answer and reliability limits.

language_observations.summary: Bold model names and numeric findings make the summary scannable, but the dense list compresses assumptions and uncertainty too aggressively.
The fit error 35.562 is called small without units or normalization, illustrating unsupported evaluative adjectives.
A concrete benchmark comparison follows the traffic estimate, but close is not quantified relative to expected historical or measurement variation.
High reliability is asserted because simulated values lie inside a reported interval, but the statistical criterion is not defined.
The strengths section repeatedly labels techniques advanced or innovative without comparative baselines or ablation evidence.

visualization_observations.summary: A banded flowchart maps preparation, two model families, methods, and sensitivity branches on one page.
The selected stair image is paired with a top-down color field and side profile to connect source appearance with derived wear depth.
visualization_observations.form: source image plus aligned field views
visualization_observations.weakness: No calibrated scale or residual view demonstrates that the color field is a measured depth map.

visualization_observations.summary: A fitted 3D surface and top-down field provide complementary views of the same spatial model.
A pedestrian-density heatmap shows a strong stripe pattern with a color scale near 10^10 while the prose reports rho=0.6535.
visualization_observations.weakness: The scale inconsistency and missing units undermine interpretation.

visualization_observations.summary: Monte Carlo points and confidence bounds visualize uncertainty but lack axes, sample definition, parameter distributions, and coverage diagnostics.
Material micrographs and a property table connect visual wear features with candidate-source parameters.
A radar chart compares heterogeneous stone properties after implicit scaling.
visualization_observations.weakness: Normalization, uncertainty, and the meaning of polygon distance are not specified.

visualization_observations.summary: One-factor sensitivity plots show shape and classification-region changes.
visualization_observations.weakness: The analysis calls large variation high sensitivity without distinguishing responsiveness from robustness.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A first-viewport workflow with explicit method handoffs may help a reviewer scan a dense multi-model solution, but this remains a within-corpus hypothesis.
alternative_explanations: The diagram may be decorative if later equations and outputs are not traceable.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: Bold numeric answers and model names are visually scannable, but award status does not prove that this formatting caused a high score.
alternative_explanations: Model breadth, topic coverage, or external judging factors may dominate formatting.

weaknesses.summary: Image-derived wear depth lacks camera/depth calibration, physical scale recovery, provenance, and a documented selection criterion.
A normalized bivariate probability density is used as physical wear depth without an explicit amplitude or unit mapping.
PSO fit error 35.562 is declared small without normalization, sample count, baseline, residual plot, or train/test separation.
The parameter k is described as both wear coefficient and friction coefficient, and the inverted traffic formula is not dimensionally justified.
Modern annual visitors are used to validate a centuries-long historical average without accounting for closures, access rules, or changing use.
The direction index depends on an unvalidated mapping from edge wear to ascent/descent and may be confounded by separate directional staircases.
The paper calls the model Navier-Stokes but supplies only continuity, no momentum closure, no velocity law, no CFL/stability analysis, and arbitrary density-flow thresholds.
Heatmap values near 10^10 are not reconciled with the reported density 0.6535, indicating a scale or implementation inconsistency.
The 100-step dataset and MSE calculation are asserted without observations, and the 0.2 decision threshold is arbitrary and unitless.
Monte Carlo distributions, correlations, sample count, random seed, and outputs are absent; interval inclusion is used circularly as reliability evidence.
The paper first declares 654-year theoretical and actual wear consistent, then uses a 312.5-year inverse estimate to infer renovation without resolving the contradiction.
Carbon-14 dating is proposed despite the problem's non-destructive and low-cost measurement constraint.
Pearson correlation across five heterogeneous material properties is not a valid source-matching method without normalization, measurement uncertainty, and a reference population.
The impulse peak-wear model and consecutive-day wear discrimination are not calibrated to detectable physical wear increments.
The conclusion omits several requested numeric answers and reliability caveats, weakening full requirement closure.

independent_extensions.label: Calibrated non-destructive measurement pipeline
independent_extensions.proposal: Use photogrammetry or structured-light scanning with scale targets, repeat scans, registration, and depth uncertainty maps; define cost and field protocol explicitly.
independent_extensions.test: Gauge repeatability, synthetic-depth recovery, perspective robustness, and blind validation against a physical reference.

independent_extensions.label: Identifiable hierarchical wear model
independent_extensions.proposal: Model wear as a function of time-varying traffic, load distribution, material coefficient, environment, and renovation change points using priors or multiple steps/sites.
independent_extensions.test: Structural identifiability, posterior predictive checks, recovery from synthetic histories, and held-out staircases.

independent_extensions.label: Pedestrian flow model with closure
independent_extensions.proposal: Use a validated fundamental diagram or social-force/continuum model with velocity closure, boundary conditions, dimensionless units, and numerical stability constraints.
independent_extensions.test: CFL check, mass conservation, lane-pattern recovery, and validation against observed trajectories.

independent_extensions.label: Metric-aware material source classification
independent_extensions.proposal: Normalize features by measurement uncertainty, compare candidate quarries using Mahalanobis or Bayesian likelihood, and include negative-source controls.
independent_extensions.test: Cross-validated source classification, calibration curves, and leave-one-quarry-out evaluation.

independent_extensions.label: Consistent age and renovation inference
independent_extensions.proposal: Fit a shared model with renovation change points so wear-consistency, age, and repair conclusions arise from one likelihood rather than separate contradictory thresholds.
independent_extensions.test: Change-point recovery, posterior odds for repair, and sensitivity to traffic-history priors.

candidate_rule_impacts.summary: The early task map supports requirement tracing, while the incomplete conclusion shows that an intro checklist alone is insufficient.
Sensitivity and Monte Carlo are present, but missing inputs and metrics strengthen the rule's validation requirements.
The paper again pairs a spatial surface with a plan view, although calibration and residual views are missing.
Small error, high reliability, and innovative are used without adequate criteria.
Every image-derived physical field requires calibration, repeatability, units, and uncertainty before entering an inverse model.
Inverse wear inference must address identifiability among age, traffic, material, environment, and renovation.
A continuum analogy requires a complete governing closure, dimensional consistency, boundary conditions, and stability tests.
Separate visual plausibility, synthetic recovery, external validation, and true holdout evidence.
Multiple estimators of the same quantity must be reconciled before one is used as evidence of repair or anomaly.
Show source image, calibrated derived field, model fit, residual field, and uncertainty as a traceable visualization chain.

unresolved_questions: What raw image, camera model, and physical calibration produced the claimed 4.5 cm wear depth?
What are the dimensions and source of the wear coefficient k, and why is it also called a friction coefficient?
Can the bivariate normal fit and PSO error be reproduced from any available data?
What velocity closure generated the pedestrian heatmap, and why is its scale near 10^10?
What distributions and sample count generated the Monte Carlo interval?
How can the 654-year wear-consistency conclusion and 312.5-year renovation conclusion both hold in one coherent model?
What actual measurements satisfy the low-cost, non-destructive, small-team constraint?
Does any later Problem A paper provide a valid inverse-wear identifiability strategy?
